title: Subsets
statement: Given an array of distinct integers, return all possible subsets (the power set). The result must not contain duplicate subsets.

nearMiss.why: DP counts or optimises; here you must list every subset, and there are 2ⁿ of them.
Subsets aren't contiguous.
There's no single best choice to commit to; every combination is required.

trigger.why: 'Return ALL …' with exponential output ⇒ backtracking: include/skip each element (bitmasks also work).

ds.answer: List<Integer> path (add / remove last) + List<List<Integer>> result
ds.why: Choose, recurse, un-choose on one path; copy it into the result.

invariant.answer: path always holds a subset of nums[0..start) in index order, and is restored after each recursive call.
wrong: path always holds exactly k elements.
path is cleared at the start of every call.
The result is added to only at the leaves of the recursion tree.
invariant.why: Adding a copy at every node of the recursion tree yields each subset exactly once.

space.why: Recursion depth and path length are at most n.

wrong: DP would return subsets in the wrong order.
DP only works when n is a power of two.

approach: backtrack(start): add copy of path; for i from start: path.add(nums[i]); backtrack(i + 1); path.removeLast().

twists.change: Count the subsets that hit a target sum instead of listing all subsets.
twists.statement: Given an array of positive integers and a target, return how many subsets have a sum exactly equal to target.
twists.trigger: how many subsets have a sum exactly equal to target
twists.ds: int[] dp of size target + 1, iterated downward per element

nearMiss.why: Listing every subset is 2ⁿ; a count over sums is pseudo-polynomial.
Enumerating bitmasks is still 2ⁿ.
Pair sums don't generalise to subsets of any size.

twists.why: Each element is in or out once, and only the running sum matters ⇒ 0/1 knapsack counting.
twists.approach: dp[0] = 1; for x: for s from target down to x: dp[s] += dp[s − x]. Return dp[target].

title: Combination Sum
statement: Given distinct positive candidates and a target, return all unique combinations whose values sum to the target. The same candidate may be used an unlimited number of times.

nearMiss.why: Unbounded knapsack DP counts combinations or checks reachability; listing every combination needs backtracking.
Two pointers find pairs with a sum; combinations here can have any length.
Taking the largest candidate first can miss valid combinations.

wrong: used an unlimited number of times
trigger.why: List every combination ⇒ backtracking; reuse ⇒ recurse with the same start index; positive values ⇒ prune when the remainder < 0.

ds.answer: List<Integer> path + List<List<Integer>> result; candidates sorted for pruning
ds.why: Sorting lets you break the loop as soon as a candidate exceeds the remainder.

invariant.answer: path is non-decreasing in candidate index, so each combination is generated once; remaining = target − sum(path).
wrong: remaining is always positive inside the recursion.
invariant.why: Only allowing indices ≥ start removes permutations of the same combination.

time.answer: Exponential: O(n^(T/m)), T = target, m = smallest candidate
time.why: Depth up to T/m, branching up to n.

space.why: The deepest path uses the smallest candidate repeatedly.

wrong: Knapsack DP doesn't allow reusing items.
Knapsack needs the target to be even.

approach: Sort. backtrack(start, remaining): if 0 record; for i from start: if c[i] > remaining break; add, backtrack(i, remaining − c[i]), remove.

twists.change: Count the combinations instead of listing them.
twists.statement: Given distinct positive candidates (each reusable) and a target, return how many combinations sum to target, ignoring order.
twists.ds: int[] dp of size target + 1, candidates in the outer loop

nearMiss.why: Listing every combination is exponential; a count is pseudo-polynomial.
With amounts in the outer loop you'd count ordered sequences; combinations need candidates outer (unbounded knapsack).
Greedy can't count.

twists.why: Unbounded knapsack counting: coins outer, sums upward.
twists.approach: dp[0] = 1; for c: for s from c to target: dp[s] += dp[s − c].

title: Word Search
statement: Given a grid of letters and a word, return true if the word can be built from letters of sequentially adjacent cells (horizontal or vertical neighbours). The same cell may not be used more than once.

nearMiss.why: Flood fill marks cells permanently; here a cell must be un-marked when a path fails, so another path can use it.
A trie helps when searching MANY words (Word Search II); one word needs only backtracking.
The 'no reuse' rule makes the state the whole path, so a grid DP table can't capture it.

trigger.answer: may not be used more than once
trigger.why: A path where visited cells must be released on the way back ⇒ DFS with choose / un-choose (backtracking).

ds.answer: The char[][] board with a temporary marker (e.g. '#') restored after recursion
wrong: boolean[][] visited that is never reset
ds.why: Marking in place and restoring is O(1) per step and needs no extra grid.

invariant.answer: Cells on the current path are marked; every cell is restored when its recursive call returns.
wrong: Once a cell is visited it is never visited again by any path.
The path always moves right or down.
The board is copied for each recursive call.
invariant.why: Restoring keeps other paths free to use the cell.

time.why: From each start, at most 3 new directions per step (you can't go back).

wrong: O(rows × cols) for a visited copy per call
space.why: Recursion depth equals the word length.

wrong: BFS/DFS can't run on letter grids.
Graph traversal would only find words in one row.
Graph traversal needs the word to be sorted.

approach: For each cell, dfs(r, c, i): bounds and board[r][c] == word[i]; if i is last return true; mark; try 4 neighbours with i + 1; restore; return result.

twists.change: Search for a whole list of words at once.
twists.statement: Given a grid of letters and a list of up to 30 000 words, return every word that can be traced through adjacent cells without reusing a cell.
twists.trigger: a list of up to 30 000 words
twists.ds: Trie of the words, with DFS over the grid walking trie nodes

nearMiss.why: Running the single-word search once per word repeats the same grid walks for shared prefixes; the trie prunes them all in one DFS.
A set of words can't tell you early that no word starts with the current path.
A plain flood fill can't reuse-check per path or stop at dead prefixes.

twists.why: Many words over one board ⇒ put the words in a trie and do one backtracking DFS that follows trie edges.
twists.approach: Build a trie; DFS from each cell following children; on a node with a word, record it (and clear it to avoid duplicates).

title: Climbing Stairs
statement: You climb a staircase of n steps, taking 1 or 2 steps at a time. In how many distinct ways can you reach the top?

nearMiss.why: Enumerating every sequence is exponential; you only need the count, and subproblems overlap.
There's nothing to optimise; it's a counting problem.
There's no bitwise structure; the count follows a Fibonacci recurrence.

wrong: taking 1 or 2 steps at a time
trigger.why: 'Number of ways' with overlapping subproblems ⇒ DP: ways(i) = ways(i − 1) + ways(i − 2).

ds.answer: Two int variables (or int[n + 1])
ds.why: Each state depends only on the two before it.

invariant.answer: ways[i] = number of distinct ways to stand on step i.
wrong: ways[i] = minimum steps to reach i.
invariant.why: The last move onto step i was a 1 (from i − 1) or a 2 (from i − 2).

time.why: One pass. (Matrix exponentiation gives O(log n), but no one expects it.)

wrong: Backtracking only works when n is even.
Backtracking would count each path twice.

approach: a = 1, b = 1 (ways to reach steps 0 and 1); repeat n − 1 times: (a, b) = (b, a + b). Return b.

twists.change: List every way, not count them.
twists.statement: You climb n stairs taking 1 or 2 steps at a time. Return every distinct sequence of step sizes that reaches the top.
twists.ds: List<Integer> path, List<List<Integer>> result, recursion on the remaining stairs

nearMiss.why: DP counts the ways (Fibonacci); listing them all means producing an exponential number of sequences anyway.
Each step is a choice in a recursion tree, not a search for reachability in a given graph.
Bitmasks don't map cleanly to sequences of varying length.

twists.why: When the output is every sequence, you choose, recurse and un-choose.
twists.approach: dfs(rem): if rem == 0 add copy; for step in {1, 2} with step ≤ rem: add, dfs(rem − step), remove.

title: House Robber
statement: Houses in a row hold given amounts of money. You cannot rob two adjacent houses. Return the maximum amount you can rob.

nearMiss.why: Taking the richest house first (or every other house) can be wrong: [2, 1, 1, 2] needs houses 0 and 3.
The chosen houses aren't contiguous; the constraint is about neighbours.
Trying every valid subset is exponential; subproblems overlap.

trigger.why: Max over a sequence of take/skip choices with a local constraint ⇒ dp[i] = max(dp[i − 1], dp[i − 2] + nums[i]).

ds.answer: Two int variables (prev, prevPrev)
ds.why: Only the last two best totals matter.

invariant.answer: best(i) = the maximum loot from houses 0..i.
invariant.why: Either skip house i (best(i − 1)) or rob it (best(i − 2) + nums[i]).

wrong: Greedy only works with an odd number of houses.
Greedy needs the amounts sorted first, which is not allowed.

approach: prev2 = 0, prev1 = 0; for x: cur = max(prev1, prev2 + x); prev2 = prev1; prev1 = cur. Return prev1.

twists.change: The houses form a binary tree; adjacent means parent and child.
twists.statement: Houses are arranged as a binary tree, each with some money. You can't rob a house and its direct parent on the same night. Return the most money you can take.
twists.ds: Recursion returning int[2] {best if robbed, best if skipped}

nearMiss.why: There is no linear order of houses; the DP runs over subtrees, post-order.
Robbing alternate levels is a tempting greedy that can be wrong (e.g. two deep rich nodes on the same branch).
Taking the richest houses first can block two richer children.

twists.why: Tree-shaped choices ⇒ post-order DFS returning both states per node (rob it / skip it).
twists.approach: f(node) = {rob = val + skip(left) + skip(right), skip = max(left) + max(right)}. Answer = max of f(root).

title: Coin Change
statement: Given coin denominations (unlimited supply of each) and an amount, return the fewest number of coins that make up that amount, or −1 if it can't be made.

nearMiss.why: Largest-coin-first fails for coins like [1, 3, 4] and amount 6 (greedy 4+1+1, optimal 3+3).
Trying every combination is exponential; the subproblem 'fewest coins for amount a' repeats.
There's no monotonic feasibility check that's easier than the DP itself.

wrong: or −1 if it can't be made
trigger.why: Minimum over choices with overlapping subproblems (amounts) ⇒ dp[a] = min over coins of dp[a − c] + 1. (BFS over amounts also works.)

ds.answer: int[amount + 1] dp filled with amount + 1 as 'infinity'
wrong: int[] dp filled with Integer.MAX_VALUE then + 1
ds.why: MAX_VALUE + 1 overflows to negative; amount + 1 is a safe infinity.

invariant.answer: dp[a] is the fewest coins that sum to exactly a, for every a computed so far.
wrong: dp[a] is the number of ways to make a.
dp[a] uses only the largest coin.
invariant.why: Computed in increasing a, so dp[a − c] is final when needed.

wrong: Greedy can't handle more than two coins.
Greedy needs the amount to be even.

approach: dp[0] = 0, others amount + 1. For a in 1..amount, for each coin ≤ a: dp[a] = min(dp[a], dp[a − c] + 1). Return dp[amount] > amount ? −1 : dp[amount].

twists.change: The coins are a canonical system: 1, 5, 10 and 25.
twists.statement: Using unlimited coins of 1, 5, 10 and 25 cents, return the fewest coins that make up a given amount.
twists.ds: Scalars: remaining amount and a coin count

nearMiss.why: The DP still works, but for this canonical system taking the largest coin first is provably optimal, so O(amount) work is unnecessary.
The unbounded-knapsack table is the general method; with these denominations no table is needed.
There's no monotonic yes/no check to search over.

twists.why: For canonical coin systems (like 1/5/10/25), the largest coin that fits is always part of an optimal answer.
twists.approach: For coin in 25, 10, 5, 1: count += amount / coin; amount %= coin.

title: Word Break
statement: Given a string s and a dictionary of words, return true if s can be segmented into a space-separated sequence of one or more dictionary words (words may be reused).

nearMiss.why: Taking the longest (or first) matching word can strand the rest: 'aaaab' style cases fail.
A trie can speed up prefix matching, but the core is still dp[i] = can s[0..i) be segmented.
Segments vary in length and must tile the whole string; there's no window property.

trigger.why: Can a prefix be built? depends on smaller prefixes ⇒ dp[i] = OR over j of dp[j] && s[j..i) in dict.

ds.answer: boolean[n + 1] dp + HashSet<String> of words
ds.why: The set makes each substring check O(length).

invariant.answer: dp[i] is true iff s[0..i) can be split into dictionary words.
wrong: dp[i] is true iff s[i] is the first letter of a word.
dp[i] counts the number of words used.
dp[i] is true iff s[0..i) is itself a single word.
invariant.why: dp[0] = true (empty prefix); answer dp[n].

time.answer: O(n² · L) (O(n · maxWordLen · L) when limiting j)
time.why: Two nested indices; substring hashing costs up to L.

wrong: Greedy only works with one dictionary word.

approach: dp[0] = true. For i in 1..n, for j < i: if dp[j] and s.substring(j, i) in set, dp[i] = true; break. Return dp[n].

twists.change: Return every possible sentence, not just whether one exists.
twists.statement: Given a string and a dictionary, return all ways to insert spaces so that every resulting word is in the dictionary.
twists.trigger: return all ways to insert spaces
twists.ds: Recursion with HashMap<Integer, List<String>> memo of sentences per start index

nearMiss.why: The boolean DP answers 'is it possible'; the output here can be exponential, so you must enumerate (memoising suffixes helps).
Word boundaries branch; two indices can't follow every split.
Words have varying lengths; there's no window rule.

twists.why: All decompositions ⇒ choose a prefix word, recurse on the rest, combine.
twists.approach: f(i): if i == n return [""]; for each word w matching at i: for s in f(i + |w|): add w + (s empty ? "" : " " + s). Memoise by i.

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
statement: Given an integer array, return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence (elements need not be adjacent). Can you do better than O(n²)?

nearMiss.why: A subsequence skips elements; sliding windows only cover contiguous runs.
A monotonic stack pops elements that may still belong to the best subsequence.
Always extending with the next larger element can lock in a poor early choice (without the tails-array refinement).

trigger.why: Best subsequence ending at each index depends on earlier ones ⇒ DP (O(n²)); the follow-up uses binary search on tails (O(n log n)).

ds.answer: int[] tails (smallest tail for each length) with binary search; or int[] dp for O(n²)
ds.why: tails stays sorted, so each element's position is a lower-bound search.

invariant.answer: tails[k] is the smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length k + 1 seen so far; tails is strictly increasing.
wrong: tails is the longest increasing subsequence itself.
tails[k] is the k-th smallest element.
tails only grows, never changes existing entries.
invariant.why: Replacing a tail with a smaller value keeps more future options open.

time.why: One binary search per element. (Plain DP is O(n²).)

wrong: Sliding windows can't handle strictly increasing values.
Sliding window needs the array sorted.
A window would count duplicates twice.

approach: For x: find the first tail ≥ x (lower bound); replace it, or append if none. Answer = tails length. (O(n²): dp[i] = 1 + max dp[j] for j < i with nums[j] < nums[i].)

twists.change: The increasing run must be contiguous.
twists.statement: Given an integer array, return the length of the longest strictly increasing contiguous subarray.
twists.ds: Two ints: current run length and best

nearMiss.why: LIS needs dp over all earlier elements (or patience sorting); a contiguous run only depends on the previous element.
Patience sorting with binary search is for subsequences; contiguity removes the need.
Nothing waits for a future greater element; the run simply resets.

twists.why: Contiguous ⇒ a running best that extends or resets at each element, like Kadane.
twists.approach: cur = 1; for i ≥ 1: cur = a[i] > a[i − 1] ? cur + 1 : 1; best = max(best, cur).

title: Longest Common Subsequence
statement: Given two strings text1 and text2, return the length of their longest common subsequence (characters in the same relative order, not necessarily contiguous).

nearMiss.why: Greedily matching characters with one pointer per string can lock in a bad match; you need to consider skipping either side.
Common characters ignore order.
Subsequences aren't contiguous; a window finds common substrings at best.

trigger.why: Two sequences compared position by position ⇒ dp[i][j] over prefixes of each.

ds.answer: int[m + 1][n + 1] table (or two rolling rows)
wrong: int[m] 1D array indexed by text1 only
ds.why: Row/column 0 represent empty prefixes.

invariant.answer: dp[i][j] is the LCS length of text1[0..i) and text2[0..j).
wrong: dp[i][j] is the LCS ending exactly at i and j.
dp[i][j] counts equal characters at the same index.
dp[i][j] is the edit distance of the prefixes.
invariant.why: Match ⇒ dp[i−1][j−1] + 1, else max(dp[i−1][j], dp[i][j−1]).

space.answer: O(m × n) (O(min(m, n)) with rolling rows)

wrong: Two pointers need both strings sorted.
Two pointers only work on equal-length strings.

approach: Fill dp row by row: if text1[i−1] == text2[j−1] then dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1] + 1 else max(dp[i−1][j], dp[i][j−1]). Return dp[m][n].

title: Edit Distance
statement: Given two words, return the minimum number of operations (insert a character, delete a character, replace a character) to convert word1 into word2.

nearMiss.why: BFS over all intermediate strings explodes; the prefix table captures the same choices in O(m × n).
Fixing the first mismatch locally (always replace) can cost more than inserting or deleting.
A single pointer per word can't explore insert vs delete vs replace together.

trigger.why: Optimal alignment of two sequences ⇒ dp[i][j] = cost for prefixes, choosing min of insert/delete/replace.

ds.answer: int[m + 1][n + 1] table with dp[i][0] = i and dp[0][j] = j
wrong: HashMap<String, Integer> memo of whole strings
ds.why: Base rows: converting to/from an empty prefix costs its length.

invariant.answer: dp[i][j] is the minimum edits to turn word1[0..i) into word2[0..j).
invariant.why: Equal chars ⇒ dp[i−1][j−1]; else 1 + min(insert dp[i][j−1], delete dp[i−1][j], replace dp[i−1][j−1]).

approach: Base row/column = index. For each cell: same char ⇒ diagonal; else 1 + min(left, up, diagonal). Return dp[m][n].

twists.change: You only need to know whether the strings are exactly one edit apart.
twists.statement: Given two strings, return true if they are exactly one edit apart: one character inserted, deleted or replaced.

nearMiss.why: The full edit-distance table is O(m · n); with a budget of one edit a single aligned walk suffices.
Character counts ignore order: "ab" vs "ba" has equal counts but is two edits apart.
There's no window over one string; both strings are walked together.

twists.why: Walk both strings until the first mismatch; the rest must match exactly after skipping one char (insert/delete) or one in each (replace).
twists.approach: If |len diff| > 1 return false. Find the first mismatch i; compare the tails s[i+1..] with t[i+1..] (same length) or with t[i..] / s[i..] (different length).

title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
statement: Given an array of positive integers, return true if it can be split into two subsets with equal sums.

nearMiss.why: Assigning each number to the currently smaller side fails on cases like [3, 3, 2, 2, 2].
Subsets aren't pairs or contiguous ranges; sorting and converging doesn't decide membership.
Trying all 2ⁿ splits is exponential; the reachable sums repeat, so DP is O(n · sum).

trigger.why: Equal halves ⇔ some subset sums to total / 2 ⇒ 0/1 subset-sum knapsack.

ds.answer: boolean[total / 2 + 1] dp iterated from high sums down
wrong: boolean[] dp iterated from low sums up
ds.why: Downward iteration ensures each number is used at most once.

invariant.answer: After processing the first i numbers, dp[s] is true iff some subset of them sums to s.
wrong: dp[s] is true iff s appears in the array.
dp[s] counts subsets summing to s.
dp is reset for every number.
invariant.why: dp[s] |= dp[s − x] adds number x to every previously reachable sum.

time.why: Pseudo-polynomial: one pass over sums per number.

wrong: Greedy only works with an even count of numbers.
Greedy needs the total to be odd.

approach: If total is odd return false. dp[0] = true; for each x, for s from target down to x: dp[s] |= dp[s − x]. Return dp[target].

twists.change: The two parts must be contiguous: one cut point.
twists.statement: Given an array of positive integers, decide whether you can cut it at a single index into a left part and a right part with equal sums.
twists.trigger: cut it at a single index
twists.ds: long total plus a running long prefix

nearMiss.why: Knapsack picks ANY subset; with one cut point there are only n − 1 candidates.
There's no choice to make greedily; you just check every cut.
There are only n − 1 cuts; enumerating subsets is unnecessary.

twists.why: Left sum = prefix, right sum = total − prefix: one pass checks every cut.
twists.approach: total = Σ; for i < n − 1: prefix += a[i]; if 2 · prefix == total return true.

title: Last Stone Weight II
statement: Stones have weights. Repeatedly smash any two stones x ≤ y: if equal both vanish, otherwise y becomes y − x. Return the smallest possible weight of the last remaining stone (0 if none remain).

nearMiss.why: Always smashing the two heaviest (Last Stone Weight I) is not optimal here; any pair may be chosen.
Local smashing choices don't minimise the final result; the real question is how to split stones into two piles.
Simulating every smash order is exponential.

trigger.answer: smallest possible weight of the last remaining stone
trigger.why: Every smash sequence ends as (sum of one group) − (sum of the other) ⇒ find the subset sum closest to total / 2: knapsack.

ds.answer: boolean[total / 2 + 1] reachable sums (iterate downward)
wrong: int[][] dp over every pair of stones
ds.why: The heap simulates version I, which is the wrong question here.

invariant.answer: dp[s] is true iff some subset of the processed stones weighs exactly s.
wrong: dp[s] is the weight left after s smashes.
dp[s] is true iff a stone weighs s.
The heaviest stone is always in the first pile.
invariant.why: Answer = total − 2 × (largest reachable s ≤ total / 2).

wrong: A heap can't hold equal weights.
A heap gives the largest stone, which is always the answer.
Heaps only work with an even number of stones.

approach: Subset-sum DP up to total / 2. Find the largest reachable s; return total − 2s.

title: Target Sum
statement: Given an array of non-negative integers and a target, put a + or − sign in front of every number. Return how many sign assignments make the expression evaluate to the target.

nearMiss.why: Prefix sums count contiguous subarrays; here every number gets a sign independently.
No single sign choice is locally best; you need a count over all assignments.
There's no pair condition to converge on.

trigger.why: P − N = target and P + N = total ⇒ count subsets with sum (total + target) / 2: 0/1 knapsack counting. (Memoised DFS also works.)

ds.answer: int[(total + target) / 2 + 1] count dp iterated downward
wrong: HashMap<String, Integer> memo of whole sign strings
ds.why: Counts, not booleans; downward for 0/1 use.

invariant.answer: After processing i numbers, dp[s] = number of subsets of them with sum s.
wrong: dp[s] = whether s equals the target.
dp[s] = number of minus signs used.
dp[s] counts each subset once per permutation.
invariant.why: dp[s] += dp[s − x] adds x to every subset counted before.

wrong: Prefix sums can't use minus signs.
Prefix sums need the array sorted.
Prefix sums only work with negative numbers.

approach: If (total + target) is odd or |target| > total return 0. P = (total + target) / 2; dp[0] = 1; for x, for s from P down to x: dp[s] += dp[s − x]. Return dp[P].

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown
statement: Given daily prices, you may complete as many transactions as you like, but after you sell you must wait one day (cooldown) before buying again, and you can hold at most one share. Return the maximum profit.

nearMiss.why: Summing every price rise works without a cooldown; the cooldown makes some rises incompatible.
Kadane's running minimum handles one transaction, not many with a cooldown rule.
A 2D table over (day, day) is unnecessary; a few states per day are enough.

trigger.answer: wait one day (cooldown) before buying again
wrong: as many transactions as you like
trigger.why: Each day you're in one of a few states (holding, just sold, resting) with restricted transitions ⇒ state-machine DP.

ds.answer: Three int variables: hold, sold, rest
ds.why: Each state updates from yesterday's states only.

invariant.answer: After day i, hold / sold / rest are the best profits ending day i in that state.
wrong: hold is the cheapest price so far.
sold is the total of all price rises.
invariant.why: hold = max(hold, rest − p); sold = hold + p; rest = max(rest, previous sold).

space.why: Three variables (save old values before updating).

wrong: Greedy can't handle prices that go down.
Greedy only works with one transaction.

approach: hold = −∞, sold = 0, rest = 0. For p: prevSold = sold; sold = hold + p; hold = max(hold, rest − p); rest = max(rest, prevSold). Return max(sold, rest).

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Transaction Fee
statement: Given daily prices and a fee charged once per completed transaction, you may trade as many times as you like but hold at most one share at a time. Return the maximum profit.

nearMiss.why: Summing every rise pays the fee on each small rise; merging rises into one trade can be better.
One running minimum handles a single transaction, not many with fees.
There are no given ranges; you're choosing when to be in or out.

trigger.answer: a fee charged once per completed transaction
wrong: as many times as you like
trigger.why: Two states (holding / not holding) with a cost on one transition ⇒ state-machine DP.

ds.answer: Two int variables: cash (not holding) and hold
ds.why: Yesterday's two states are enough.

invariant.answer: cash = best profit ending today without a share; hold = best profit ending today holding one.
wrong: hold only changes on price drops.
The fee is paid on both buy and sell.
invariant.why: cash = max(cash, hold + p − fee); hold = max(hold, cash − p).

wrong: Greedy needs the fee to be zero to run at all.
Greedy only works on increasing prices.

approach: cash = 0, hold = −prices[0]. For p: cash = max(cash, hold + p − fee); hold = max(hold, cash − p). Return cash.

title: Permutations
statement: Given an array of distinct integers, return every possible ordering of all its elements.

nearMiss.why: Nothing is counted or optimised; every ordering must be listed, so the output is n! long anyway.
Bitmasks enumerate SUBSETS; orderings need a position-by-position choice (a mask can track 'used', but the search is still backtracking).
There's no input graph; the recursion tree of choices is the search space.

trigger.why: Enumerate all arrangements ⇒ choose, recurse, un-choose.

ds.answer: List<Integer> path, boolean[] used, List<List<Integer>> result
ds.why: Copy path into result when it reaches length n.

invariant.answer: path holds a partial ordering of distinct unused values; used[i] is true exactly for the elements in path.
wrong: Each recursive level removes the smallest value.
used is reset to false at every level.
invariant.why: Undo the choice after recursing.

time.why: n! leaves, each copied in O(n).

wrong: DP would return only the sorted permutation.
DP needs the array sorted first.

approach: dfs(): if path.size() == n add copy; for each i not used: mark, add, dfs, remove, unmark.

twists.change: Given one ordering, produce only the next one in lexicographic order, in place.
twists.statement: Given an arrangement of integers, rearrange it in place into the next lexicographically greater permutation (or the smallest if it is the last).
twists.ds: int indices on the array; swap and reverse

nearMiss.why: Generating all permutations to find the next one is n!; the next one differs only in a suffix.
The decreasing suffix is found by a simple scan; no stack is needed.
Nothing is split around a pivot value.

twists.why: Find the rightmost ascent i, swap a[i] with the smallest larger value to its right, reverse the suffix.
twists.approach: i from n − 2 while a[i] ≥ a[i + 1]; if i ≥ 0 find j > i rightmost with a[j] > a[i], swap; reverse a[i + 1..].

title: N-Queens
statement: Place n queens on an n × n chessboard so that no two attack each other (same row, column or diagonal). Return all distinct board configurations.

nearMiss.why: Placements interact across whole columns and diagonals, so there's no small state to tabulate; we must list boards.
Placing each queen in the first safe column can dead-end; you have to undo choices.
There's no in-place traversal trick; the board is a search space.

trigger.why: Place one queen per row with constraint checks and undo on failure ⇒ backtracking with pruning.

ds.answer: boolean[] cols, boolean[] diag (r + c), boolean[] antiDiag (r − c + n − 1); char[][] board
wrong: HashSet<String> of boards checked at the end
ds.why: O(1) attack checks per placement.

invariant.answer: Rows 0..r − 1 each hold exactly one queen and no two of them attack; the three arrays mark exactly the attacked columns and diagonals.
wrong: Every column already has a queen.
Queens are always placed on the main diagonal.
The board is valid only once all queens are placed.
invariant.why: Pruning early keeps the search far below n^n.

time.why: At most n choices in row 0, n − 1 safe ones in row 1, and so on.

space.answer: O(n²) for the board (O(n) for the bookkeeping)
space.why: Board, three flag arrays, recursion depth n.

wrong: DP would place all queens in one row.
DP only works when n is even.

approach: place(r): if r == n record the board; for c: if free, mark col/diag/anti, put 'Q', place(r + 1), undo.

title: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
statement: Each digit 2–9 maps to a few letters as on a phone keypad. Given a string of such digits, return every letter string the digits could represent.

nearMiss.why: Nothing to count or optimise; every combination is part of the output.
The digit → letters map is a lookup table, but producing all combinations is the search.
There's no pair to converge on; each position is an independent choice.

trigger.answer: every letter string the digits could represent
wrong: Each digit 2–9 maps to a few letters
trigger.why: Cartesian product of choices per position ⇒ backtracking (or iterative BFS-style expansion).

ds.answer: String[] keypad, StringBuilder path, List<String> result
ds.why: Append, recurse, delete last char.

invariant.answer: path holds one letter for each digit processed so far, in order.
wrong: path always has the same length as digits.
Each letter is used only once overall.
Results are sorted lexicographically by construction.
invariant.why: Record when path length == digits length.

time.why: Up to 4 letters per digit, each result built in O(n).

wrong: DP would return only one combination.

approach: dfs(i): if i == n add path; for each letter of keypad[digits[i]]: append, dfs(i + 1), remove last. Return [] for empty input.

title: Generate Parentheses
statement: Given n, return every string of n pairs of parentheses that is well-formed.

nearMiss.why: A stack VALIDATES one string; here we generate them, and two counters (open, close) replace the stack.
DP over Catalan splits can build them, but the standard recognisable approach is pruned backtracking on counts.
Enumerating all 2^(2n) bit strings and filtering wastes nearly all the work.

trigger.answer: every string of n pairs of parentheses
trigger.why: Generate all valid strings ⇒ backtrack, adding '(' while open < n and ')' while close < open.

ds.answer: StringBuilder path, ints open and close, List<String> result
ds.why: The counts are the whole state.

invariant.answer: Every prefix built has close ≤ open ≤ n, so it can always be completed to a valid string.
wrong: Strings are generated in sorted order by length.
invariant.why: Pruning means no dead branches.

wrong: A stack would generate only one string.

approach: dfs(open, close): if length == 2n add; if open < n add '(' and recurse; if close < open add ')' and recurse; undo each.

twists.change: Count the valid strings instead of listing them.
twists.statement: Given n, return how many strings of n pairs of parentheses are well-formed.
twists.ds: long[] dp of size n + 1 (Catalan numbers)

nearMiss.why: Listing each string costs the Catalan number of leaves; counting needs only a recurrence.
A stack validates one string; it doesn't count them.
There's no capacity; the recurrence splits on the first pair's matching position.

twists.why: dp[n] = Σ dp[i] · dp[n − 1 − i]: the first '(' closes after i inner pairs.
twists.approach: dp[0] = 1; for k in 1..n: for i in 0..k−1: dp[k] += dp[i] · dp[k − 1 − i].

title: Decode Ways
statement: Letters A–Z are encoded as "1"–"26". Given a digit string, return the number of ways to decode it into letters. A '0' can only appear as part of "10" or "20".

nearMiss.why: Listing every decoding is exponential; we only need the count, and the same suffixes recur.
Always taking two digits (or one) can break later decodings or miss valid ones.
There's no nesting to match; each choice depends only on the previous one or two digits.

trigger.answer: return the number of ways to decode it
trigger.why: Count ways where each step uses 1 or 2 characters ⇒ dp[i] = dp[i−1] (if valid single) + dp[i−2] (if valid pair).

ds.answer: int[] dp of size n + 1 (or two rolling ints)
ds.why: Climbing-stairs shape with validity checks.

invariant.answer: dp[i] is the number of ways to decode the first i characters.
wrong: dp[i] is the number of letters in the decoding.
dp[i] counts decodings that end with a two-digit code.
invariant.why: dp[0] = 1 (empty string); a '0' that can't pair makes dp zero from there.

space.why: Only dp[i−1] and dp[i−2] are needed.

title: House Robber II
statement: Houses with given amounts of money stand in a circle, so the first and last are neighbours. You can't rob two adjacent houses. Return the most money you can take.

nearMiss.why: Taking the richest houses first can block better combinations.
There's no multi-state machine here; the circle is handled by solving two linear cases.
Kadane picks one contiguous run; here picks must be non-adjacent.

trigger.answer: the first and last are neighbours
trigger.why: Circle ⇒ either skip the first house or skip the last; run House Robber on each line and take the max.

ds.answer: Two rolling ints (prev, cur) per linear run
ds.why: O(1) space per run.

invariant.answer: For a linear run, best(i) = max(best(i − 1), best(i − 2) + money[i]); the circular answer is max(run on 0..n−2, run on 1..n−1).
wrong: The first house is always robbed.
invariant.why: No optimal plan uses both the first and last house.

wrong: Greedy needs sorted amounts, and sorting breaks adjacency only sometimes.

approach: If n == 1 return money[0]. Return max(rob(0, n − 2), rob(1, n − 1)), where rob is the linear two-variable DP.

title: Unique Paths
statement: A robot starts at the top-left of an m × n grid and can only move right or down. Count the distinct paths that reach the bottom-right cell.

nearMiss.why: DFS/BFS would enumerate every path one by one, which is exponential; we only need the count.
Listing paths is exponential; overlapping subproblems make counting polynomial.
The rolled-up implementation uses one row, but the recurrence is over a 2-D grid of states (r, c).

trigger.answer: can only move right or down
trigger.why: Monotone moves on a grid ⇒ paths(r, c) = paths(r − 1, c) + paths(r, c − 1).

ds.answer: int[m][n] table (or one int[] row of size n)
ds.why: Row-by-row fill, left to right.

invariant.answer: dp[r][c] is the number of paths from the start to (r, c); the first row and column are all 1.
wrong: dp[r][c] is the shortest distance to (r, c).
invariant.why: Each path to (r, c) arrives from above or from the left.

time.why: Each cell once. (A binomial formula also gives O(min(m, n)).)

space.why: Only the previous row is needed.

wrong: BFS can't count; it can only find one path.

approach: row = all 1s; for r in 1..m−1, for c in 1..n−1: row[c] += row[c − 1]. Return row[n − 1].

twists.change: Return every path, not the count.
twists.statement: A robot moves only right or down on an m × n grid from the top-left to the bottom-right. Return every path as a string of 'R' and 'D' moves.
twists.ds: StringBuilder path, List<String> result, recursion on (r, c)

nearMiss.why: The table counts paths; it can't list C(m + n − 2, m − 1) of them without enumerating anyway.
Distances don't matter; every path is output.
Enumerating all 2^(m + n − 2) bit strings and filtering wastes most of the work.

twists.why: Output is every sequence of choices ⇒ backtracking.
twists.approach: dfs(r, c): at target add path; if r < m − 1 append 'D', recurse, delete; if c < n − 1 append 'R', recurse, delete.

title: Minimum Path Sum
statement: Given an m × n grid of non-negative numbers, find a path from the top-left to the bottom-right that minimises the sum of the numbers along it. You may only move right or down.

nearMiss.why: Dijkstra works but costs a log factor; with only right/down moves the grid is a DAG with an obvious fill order.
Taking the cheaper next cell can lead into an expensive region later.
Plain BFS ignores cell weights.

trigger.answer: You may only move right or down
wrong: minimises the sum of the numbers along it
trigger.why: Right/down only ⇒ acyclic grid ⇒ dp[r][c] = grid[r][c] + min(top, left).

ds.answer: int[m][n] table, or update the grid / one row in place
ds.why: In-place updates make it O(1) extra space.

invariant.answer: dp[r][c] is the minimum path sum from the start to (r, c).
wrong: dp[r][c] is the number of paths to (r, c).
The minimum path always follows the first row then the last column.
invariant.why: Both predecessors are already final when (r, c) is filled.

space.answer: O(n) with one row (O(1) in place)
space.why: Only the previous row is needed.

wrong: Dijkstra would give the maximum sum.

approach: row[0] = grid[0][0]; fill the first row cumulatively; for each later row: row[0] += grid[r][0]; row[c] = grid[r][c] + min(row[c], row[c − 1]).

twists.change: You may now move in all four directions.
twists.statement: Given an m × n grid of non-negative costs, find the cheapest path from the top-left to the bottom-right, where you may move up, down, left or right. The path cost is the sum of the cells on it.
twists.trigger: move up, down, left or right
twists.ds: PriorityQueue<int[]> of {cost, r, c} and int[][] best

nearMiss.why: With moves in all four directions there's no acyclic fill order; a cell's best may come from below or the right.
Plain BFS ignores the cell weights.
One source, and edges aren't unit-weight.

twists.why: Non-negative weights on a graph with cycles ⇒ Dijkstra.
twists.approach: Dijkstra from (0, 0) with cost grid[0][0]; relax neighbours with cost + grid[nr][nc].

title: Maximal Square
statement: In a binary matrix of '0' and '1', find the largest square containing only '1's and return its area.

nearMiss.why: Row-by-row histograms with a monotonic stack solve maximal RECTANGLE; for squares a simpler DP suffices.
Connected regions of 1s needn't be square; flood fill measures the wrong thing.
2-D prefix sums can test any square in O(1), but trying all squares is still O(m · n · min(m, n)).

trigger.why: Square ending at (r, c) is limited by its top, left and top-left neighbours ⇒ dp = 1 + min of the three.

ds.answer: int[m + 1][n + 1] table (or one row plus a 'diagonal' int)
ds.why: Padding removes edge checks.

invariant.answer: dp[r][c] is the side of the largest all-'1' square whose bottom-right corner is (r, c).
wrong: dp[r][c] is the number of 1s above (r, c).
dp[r][c] = dp[r − 1][c − 1] + 1 whenever the cell is '1'.
dp[r][c] is the area of the square.
invariant.why: Track the max side; answer is side².

wrong: A monotonic stack would only find 1 × 1 squares.

approach: If cell == '1': dp[r+1][c+1] = 1 + min(dp[r][c+1], dp[r+1][c], dp[r][c]); track best side; return best².

title: Coin Change II
statement: Given coin denominations (unlimited supply of each) and an amount, return the number of combinations that make up that amount. Order doesn't matter: 1+2 and 2+1 are the same combination.

nearMiss.why: Coin Change I (fewest coins) is a 1-D DP over amounts; COUNTING combinations needs the knapsack loop order (coins outer) so orderings aren't double-counted.
Enumerating combinations is exponential; we only need the count.
Greedy finds one way at best; it can't count all of them.

trigger.why: Unbounded knapsack count: iterate coins in the OUTER loop and amounts upward, so each combination is counted once.

ds.answer: int[] dp of size amount + 1, dp[0] = 1
wrong: int[] dp with amounts in the outer loop and coins inner
ds.why: Amounts outer would count permutations (that's Combination Sum IV).

invariant.answer: After processing the first j coins, dp[a] is the number of combinations of those coins that sum to a.
wrong: dp[a] is the fewest coins for amount a.
invariant.why: Upward iteration over a allows reusing the current coin (unbounded).

wrong: 1-D DP would need the coins sorted descending.
1-D DP only works when all coins are distinct.

approach: dp[0] = 1; for coin: for a from coin to amount: dp[a] += dp[a − coin]. Return dp[amount].

twists.change: Order now matters: 1+2 and 2+1 count separately.
twists.statement: Given distinct positive numbers (each usable any number of times) and a target, return how many ordered sequences of them sum to target.

nearMiss.why: The knapsack loop order (items outer) counts each combination once; ordered sequences need amounts outer, items inner.
Listing sequences is exponential; only the count is needed.
Greedy can't count.

twists.why: Ordered ⇒ dp[t] = Σ dp[t − x] over every number x: the last element can be any of them.
twists.approach: dp[0] = 1; for t in 1..target: for x: if x ≤ t, dp[t] += dp[t − x].

title: Ones and Zeroes
statement: Given binary strings and limits m and n, return the size of the largest subset of the strings whose total count of 0s is at most m and total count of 1s is at most n.

nearMiss.why: Picking the shortest strings first fails: a string heavy in 0s can block several strings that only need 1s.
Trying every subset is 2^k; the capacities are small enough to tabulate.
The table is 2-D, but it's over two CAPACITIES of a 0/1 item choice, which is knapsack, not two sequences or a grid.

trigger.answer: total count of 0s is at most m and total count of 1s is at most n
trigger.why: Each string is a 0/1 item with a two-dimensional weight (zeros, ones) ⇒ 0/1 knapsack with two capacities, iterated downward.

ds.answer: int[m + 1][n + 1] dp, iterated downward in both capacities per string
wrong: int[m + 1][n + 1] iterated upward in both capacities
ds.why: Downward iteration keeps each string used at most once.

invariant.answer: After processing some strings, dp[i][j] is the largest subset of them using at most i zeros and j ones.
wrong: dp[i][j] is the number of strings with i zeros and j ones.
dp[i][j] only increases when i == j.
Each string can be counted more than once.
invariant.why: dp[i][j] = max(dp[i][j], dp[i − z][j − o] + 1).

time.answer: O(k · m · n) plus the counting
time.why: Each string updates the whole table.

wrong: 2-D DP needs the strings sorted by length.
2-D DP would let each string be used once only, which is wrong.

approach: For each string count z, o; for i from m down to z, for j from n down to o: dp[i][j] = max(dp[i][j], dp[i − z][j − o] + 1).

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock III
statement: Given daily stock prices, find the maximum profit with at most two transactions. You must sell before buying again.

nearMiss.why: One pass of running min/max handles ONE transaction; with two, you need separate states for each buy and sell.
Summing every rising step allows unlimited transactions, which overshoots the limit of two.
Best-left/best-right split arrays do work (a valid variant), but they're the state machine unrolled; the recognisable shape is states per transaction.

trigger.why: A fixed number of buy/sell steps ⇒ states buy1, sell1, buy2, sell2 updated each day.

ds.answer: Four ints: buy1, sell1, buy2, sell2
wrong: int[][] dp[i][j] over every day pair
ds.why: Each state depends only on the previous day's states.

invariant.answer: Each variable is the best cash after that step (first buy, first sell, second buy, second sell) on any day so far.
wrong: buy2 is always the second-lowest price.
The states only change on price drops.
invariant.why: buy2 = max(buy2, sell1 − p) chains the second transaction to the first.

wrong: Kadane would give the minimum profit.

approach: buy1 = buy2 = −∞; for p: buy1 = max(buy1, −p); sell1 = max(sell1, buy1 + p); buy2 = max(buy2, sell1 − p); sell2 = max(sell2, buy2 + p). Return sell2.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II
statement: Given daily stock prices, you may hold at most one share at a time but may buy and sell as many times as you like (even on the same day). Return the maximum profit.

nearMiss.why: Running min/max finds the single best transaction, which ignores the other profitable rises.
Pairing peaks and valleys with a stack works, but summing positive day-to-day differences is simpler.
There's no single pair to find; the profit is a sum over many pairs.

trigger.answer: as many times as you like
wrong: at most one share at a time
trigger.why: Unlimited transactions ⇒ two states (hold / cash), which collapses to summing every positive daily rise.

ds.answer: Two ints: hold and cash (or one profit sum)
ds.why: O(1) space.

invariant.answer: cash is the best profit with no share at the end of day i; hold is the best with one share.
wrong: hold is always the lowest price seen.
cash only changes on the last day.
Each day is either a buy or a sell.
invariant.why: Equivalently: profit += max(0, p[i] − p[i − 1]).

wrong: Kadane can't handle more than ten days.
Kadane only works on negative numbers.
Kadane would give a larger profit than is possible.

approach: cash = 0, hold = −p[0]; for p: cash = max(cash, hold + p); hold = max(hold, cash − p). Return cash. (Or sum positive differences.)
